# Using videos in Remotion

## Prerequisites

First, the @remotion/media package needs to be installed.  
If it is not, use the following command:

```bash
npx remotion add @remotion/media # If project uses npm
bunx remotion add @remotion/media # If project uses bun
yarn remotion add @remotion/media # If project uses yarn
pnpm exec remotion add @remotion/media # If project uses pnpm
```

Use `<Video>` from `@remotion/media` to embed videos into your composition.

```tsx
import { Video } from "@remotion/media";
import { staticFile } from "remotion";

export const MyComposition = () => {
  return <Video src={staticFile("video.mp4")} />;
};
```

Remote URLs are also supported:

```tsx
<Video src="https://remotion.media/video.mp4" />
```

## Trimming

Use `trimBefore` and `trimAfter` to remove portions of the video. Values are in seconds.

```tsx
const { fps } = useVideoConfig();

return (
  <Video
    src={staticFile("video.mp4")}
    trimBefore={2 * fps} // Skip the first 2 seconds
    trimAfter={10 * fps} // End at the 10 second mark
  />
);
```

## Delaying

Wrap the video in a `<Sequence>` to delay when it appears:

```tsx
import { Sequence, staticFile } from "remotion";

content.content:
# Authentication

Most web apps require authentication. Testreel supports several approaches so your recordings start in a logged-in state without capturing the login flow on video.

## Setup block (recommended)

The `setup` block runs steps **before** video recording starts. Session state (cookies, localStorage, etc.) is automatically carried over into the recorded session.

```json
{
  "url": "https://app.example.com/dashboard",
  "setup": {
    "url": "https://app.example.com/login",
    "steps": [
      { "action": "fill", "selector": "#email", "text": "user@example.com" },
      { "action": "fill", "selector": "#password", "text": "s3cret" },
      { "action": "click", "selector": "button[type=submit]" },
      { "action": "wait", "ms": 2000 }
    ]
  },
  "steps": [
    { "action": "screenshot", "name": "dashboard" }
  ]
}
```

The setup block accepts:
- `url` (optional) — the page to navigate to for setup. Defaults to the main `url`.
- `steps` — same actions as the recording. Cursor is disabled during setup.

Setup also preserves scroll position — if your setup scrolls to a specific section, the recording starts at that position.

You can also provide setup in a separate file via the CLI:

```bash
npx testreel recording.json --setup login-steps.json
```

## localStorage injection

For apps that store auth tokens in localStorage (e.g., Supabase, Firebase):

```json
{
  "url": "https://app.example.com",
  "localStorage": {
    "sb-auth-token": "{\"access_token\":\"eyJ...\",\"refresh_token\":\"abc\"}"
  },
  "steps": [...]
}
```

Testreel navigates to the URL, injects the entries, then reloads to let the app pick up the session.

## Cookies

```json
{
  "url": "https://app.example.com",
  "cookies": [
    {
      "name": "session",
      "value": "abc123",
      "domain": "app.example.com",
      "path": "/"
    }
  ],
  "steps": [...]
}
```

```

## Interactive login (`testreel login`)

For OAuth flows or other logins that are hard to automate, use the `login` subcommand. It opens a real browser, lets you log in manually, and exports the session state to a JSON file.

```bash
# Open a browser, log in, then close the window to save
npx testreel login https://app.example.com --save-state ./state.json

# Use Chrome instead of Chromium (needed for Google OAuth and other
# providers that block automation-controlled browsers)
npx testreel login https://app.example.com --save-state ./state.json --channel chrome

# Connect to an already-running browser via CDP
npx testreel login https://app.example.com --save-state ./state.json --cdp http://localhost:9222

# Headless login with a web-based viewer (useful on remote/CI machines)
npx testreel login https://app.example.com --save-state ./state.json --remote
```

Then reference the saved state in your recording definition:

```json
{
  "url": "https://app.example.com",
  "storageState": "./state.json",
  "steps": [...]
}
```

## Playwright storage state

If you already have a Playwright `storageState` JSON file (from `context.storageState()`), point to it directly:

```json
{
  "url": "https://app.example.com",
  "storageState": "./auth-state.json",
  "steps": [...]
}
```

## Extra headers

For APIs or apps that accept auth headers (e.g., Bearer tokens):

```json
{
  "url": "https://app.example.com",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer eyJ..."
  },
  "steps": [...]
}
```

## Supabase auth provider

For Supabase-based apps, testreel can generate a session automatically using a service role key:

```json
{
  "url": "https://app.example.com",
  "auth": {
    "provider": "supabase",
    "url": "${SUPABASE_URL}",
    "serviceRoleKey": "${SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY}",
    "email": "${TEST_USER_EMAIL}"
  },
  "steps": [...]

# Browser-driven verification (authenticated)

For any UI verification that needs a signed-in session (past the auth wall), mint a session cookie from the DB and drive the **paired Owletto extension** through the Lobu connector-operations bridge (`lobu call manage_operations`, or the SDK `operations` namespace). This runs in the user's real logged-in Chrome — no separate headless browser, no CDP, no extra browser tooling to install.

## Scope

The forged session cookie authenticates the **web admin REST mounted at `/`** (`/api/auth/*`, `/api/<orgSlug>/...`, the SPA — anything `lobu apply` and the web app talk to). It does **NOT** authenticate the **public Agent API at `/lobu`** (`/lobu/api/v1/agents/*`, `/lobu/api/v1/agents/<id>/sessions`) — that path expects a JWT bearer from the OAuth device flow (`lobu login`) or a PAT. If `/lobu/api/v1/agents` returns `401` despite a valid cookie, switch to `lobu chat` / `lobu token`.

## Pick a target

Local dev backend (with prod DB attached over Tailscale): `https://<your-tailscale-host>.ts.net:8443`. Prod: `https://app.lobu.ai`.

## Grab the secret + session token

```bash
# Local dev backend uses .env's BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
SECRET=$(grep '^BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)

# Prod uses the secret on the K8s pod
SECRET=$(kubectl exec -n summaries-prod \
  $(kubectl get pod -n summaries-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=lobu-app -o name | head -1 | sed 's|pod/||') \
  -- printenv BETTER_AUTH_SECRET)
```

Session token from the DB. With no local `DATABASE_URL` set, exec psql inside the prod DB pod (the prod DB serves both targets):

```bash
DBURL=$(kubectl exec -n summaries-prod <lobu-app-pod> -- printenv DATABASE_URL)
PGPASS=$(printf '%s' "$DBURL" | sed -E 's#.*://[^:]+:([^@]+)@.*#\1#')
TOKEN=$(kubectl exec -n summaries-prod lobu-ai-prod-db-1 -- \
  env PGPASSWORD="REDACTED" psql -h lobu-ai-prod-db-pooler -U summaries -d owletto -tAc \
  "SELECT token FROM session WHERE \"userId\" = '<user_id>' AND \"expiresAt\" > NOW() ORDER BY \"updatedAt\" DESC LIMIT 1")
```

## Sign the cookie

better-auth uses HMAC-SHA256, base64, then URL-encode — base64**url** does *not* validate.

```bash
SIGNED=$(SECRET="$SECRET" TOKEN="$TOKEN" node -e '
  const {createHmac}=require("node:crypto");
  const sig=createHmac("sha256",process.env.SECRET).update(process.env.TOKEN).digest("base64");
  console.log(encodeURIComponent(`${process.env.TOKEN}.${sig}`));
')
```

Cookie name is `__Secure-better-auth.session_token` whenever the baseURL is `https://` (prod and Tailscale dev qualify; only plain-http localhost uses the unprefixed `better-auth.session_token`).

## Find the Chrome connection

Browser actions dispatch to a paired Chrome extension connection (usually org `buremba`):

```bash
lobu call manage_connections --org buremba --arg action=list --raw
```

Pick the `chrome` connector with `status: active` on the machine whose browser you want to drive. `operations.listAvailable({ connection_id })` reports per-target `readiness` and `execution_targets` — use it to check the device is actually online before a long verification.

## Drive the browser

Multi-step verifications are one `run_sdk` script (the tab id threads through every call):

```bash
lobu call run_sdk --arg script='
export default async (ctx, client) => {
  const CHROME = <chrome-connection-id>;
  const COOKIE = "<SIGNED>";
  // 1. Open the app origin in a fresh background tab.
  const nav = await client.operations.execute({
    connection_id: CHROME, operation_key: "navigate",

---
name: reference_owletto_bridge_and_localhost_auth
description: "How to get an authenticated browser for UI verification — Owletto bridge for prod, and the PAT-exchange-through-vite-proxy recipe for running local SPA code against the prod API (forged cookies DO NOT work)"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: dc1df443-8162-4cd9-b062-3e67f86994ab
  modified: 2026-07-30T16:24:42.893Z
---

Measured 2026-07-30 while verifying the Behavior authoring rework (owletto#634).

**The forged-cookie recipe in `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md` no longer authenticates.** HMAC-signing a
`session` row token with `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` and setting
`__Secure-better-auth.session_token` returns `null` from `/api/auth/get-session` — verified with
curl straight at `https://app.lobu.ai`, not just through a proxy. The signing format still matches
`mintSessionCookieValue` in `packages/server/src/auth/routes.ts` exactly, so something else rejects
it. Don't burn a session re-deriving the signature.

**What works instead — PAT exchange:**

```bash

Yes — and I should have gone here instead of fighting a 127 MB headless Chromium download. I have a standing instruction to use the paired Owletto extension and not spin up a separate headless browser, and I ignored it.

Here's what's actually live on the bridge right now (queried, not assumed):

| Connection | Ops |
|---|---|
| `chrome` ×2 (479, 432) | `navigate`, `click_ref`, `type_ref`, `wait_for_selector`, `evaluate`, `screenshot`, `get_accessibility_tree` |
| `apple.computer_use` (447) | `click`, `move_mouse`, `type_text`, `launch_app`, `focus_window`, `list_windows` |
| `os.shell` (464) | `run` |

That changes the plan more than I first credited, in three ways:

**Auth stops being a problem.** The bridge drives your *already logged-in* Chrome. No storageState export, no cookie forging (which the memory says stopped working anyway), no login step I'm not allowed to perform.

**Native Slack and a real terminal become recordable.** `apple.computer_use` drives the desktop, not just a browser. Playwright fundamentally cannot touch either. That kills the brainless re-enactment compromise outright — beats 2 and 4 become real Claude Code and real Codex, not a replay.

**Recording is `os.shell run`.** The bridge drives but doesn't record; the recorder is a native macOS screen capture started and stopped over the shell connection.

Two honest gaps before this works:

`os.shell` was last seen **2026-08-01** — five days ago, so it's almost certainly offline. Both Chromes were seen ~4h ago, `computer_use` ~9h ago. So the driving half is live and the recording half isn't.

And the reason the mini matters isn't automation, it's framing: a full-screen capture records whatever is on that desktop. On a mini with a demo account that's a feature. On your daily machine it's a liability — every notification, every tab title, every real customer name ends up in the video.

What survives from tonight: the Remotion composition layer is unaffected and still correct — camera, packets, captions, the table. It doesn't care where the footage comes from. What gets dropped is testreel and the four `capture/ui-*.json` definitions I just wrote for it.

So: **is the mini set up and paired, or is that still to do?** That's the fork I can't resolve — if it's paired I need its `os.shell` online and I can start capturing tonight; if not, the fastest real footage is the Chrome bridge against your laptop for the *Lobu UI beats only*, where I can frame the window and never capture the full desktop.

**Confidence: high (~90)** on the ops inventory — that's a live query against the bridge, not documentation. **Low (~30)** that this works end-to-end tonight, because `os.shell` looks stale and I haven't verified Screen Recording permission on any target machine.

Next actions you can pick from:
- Tell me which machine, and bring `os.shell` online there — then I'll test the capture start/stop loop with a 5-second throwaway before anything real.
- If the mini's not ready: I drive the Chrome bridge on your laptop and capture just the Lobu UI beats, window-framed, no full desktop.
- Either way, seed the demo org first — the map beat is four pages, and four empty pages is worse footage than grey boxes.
- Decide the cursor question: `click_ref` leaves no visible pointer, so beats 2a and 5 either use `computer_use`'s `move_mouse` or get a synthesized Remotion cursor.

That settles it — you're right, and the permission map is exact:

```
kTCCServiceScreenCapture | com.owletto.mac              | 2  ← GRANTED
kTCCServiceAccessibility | com.owletto.mac              | 2  ← GRANTED
kTCCServiceScreenCapture | com.apple.Terminal           | 2  ← GRANTED
kTCCServiceAccessibility | /usr/libexec/sshd-keygen-wrapper | 0  ← DENIED
```

Owletto has both. SSH has neither — that's why my `screencapture` failed and why peekaboo reported "Not Granted". The permission isn't missing, it's just not mine to use over SSH.

## The trap: `log` is shadowed in this shell

There is a zsh function named `log` on this machine. Every `log show …` invocation
hits it, not `/usr/bin/log`, and it fails with:

    (eval):log:1: too many arguments

With `2>/dev/null` on the command — which is the natural thing to write — this
looks like **an empty result set**, not an error. It cost a wrong conclusion
("the Mac app emits no logs at all") that survived three separate predicates and
got as far as being reported to the user. There were 79,897 lines.

**Always use `/usr/bin/log show`, and never suppress stderr on a diagnostic
command whose empty output you intend to reason from.** An absence you can't
distinguish from an error is not evidence — same family as
[[feedback_absence_needs_origin_main_grep]].

Useful predicates once you're calling the real binary:

    /usr/bin/log show --last 3h --predicate 'process == "Owletto"' --style compact
    /usr/bin/log show --last 3h --predicate 'subsystem == "ai.lobu.mac"' --info --debug

## How the Mac app logs (as of owletto `feat/mac-perms-logging`)

`apps/mac/Owletto/Log.swift` — `Log.info/.error/.debug(_ category:, _ message:)`.

```
21:40:19 [ERROR] [sync] sync error: Worker /api/workers/poll failed (503): no available server
21:43:58 [INFO]  [worker] executing run          ← os.shell WORKS
21:44:18 [INFO]  [worker] executing observe      ← then nothing, ever again

The capture path works end to end. You were right and I was building the wrong thing.

**What's proven:** a screen recording issued through Owletto's `os.shell` returns h264, **1920×1080, 60 fps** — my composition resolution and framerate, natively, with zero scaling. No headless Chromium, no storageState, no cookie forging. The 2.18 MB PNG and 905 KB mov were real pixels, not black frames.

**What was actually broken:** the mini's device worker had been dark for 5 hours. The log showed it taking a `503 no available server` on `/api/workers/poll` at 21:40 UTC, executing two more operations, then stopping forever at 21:44 — while the process stayed up for 25 hours looking healthy. Restarting it brought back `capabilities=[computer_use, os.shell, reminders]`. That's a real bug worth filing separately: **the poll loop doesn't recover from a 503, and the device goes silently dark rather than reporting unhealthy.**

Three things you need to know before we shoot:

**There's a permission dialog on the mini's screen right now** — "Owletto would like to access data from other apps" — triggered by my restart. It's waiting on a click, and granting permissions isn't something I'll do on your behalf. It also needs clearing because it's currently *in frame*.

**The desktop isn't shootable.** The capture shows roughly sixty files on it, almost all screenshots, plus the dock and menu bar. All of that lands in the video. This is the thing the demo user account was always for.

**The 60 fps claim isn't verified under motion.** The container declares 60/1 but only 45 frames landed in 5 seconds — expected on a frozen desktop, since there's nothing to encode, but I haven't tested it with something actually moving. That's a real risk for a film built on 320 ms camera moves.

Dropping testreel and the four `capture/ui-*.json` files I wrote for it. The Remotion composition layer is unaffected — it doesn't care where footage comes from.

**Confidence: high (~90)** that the capture path works — I ran it and probed the output, rather than reasoning about it. **Low (~35)** on frame rate under motion, which is the next thing to test and the one that could still force a rethink.

Next actions you can pick from:
- Dismiss that Owletto dialog on the mini so the screen is clean.
- Let me run a motion fps test — open something animating, record 5 s, count real frames. If it doesn't hold 60, we find out now rather than after a day of capture.

- Want me to file the device-goes-dark-after-503 bug? It's unrelated to the video but it's a genuine production issue and I have the log evidence.

content.text:
Blocked, and it's a permission grant that's yours to make, not mine.

There's a dialog sitting on the mini's screen right now:

> **"Owletto" wants access to control "System Events."** Allowing control will provide access to documents and data in "System Events", and to perform actions within that app.

That's what stalled the 63-second command — `osascript` blocked waiting for someone at the machine. I won't click Allow on your behalf; granting permissions is your call.

Two ways forward, and I'd take the second:

**Click Allow**, and AppleScript control works. But it widens Owletto's permissions permanently for a demo video.

**Skip AppleScript entirely.** Owletto already has `computer_use` ops — `hotkey`, `focus_window`, `move_mouse`, `click`, `launch_app` — that do the same jobs through its own granted Accessibility permission, no new consent needed. That was the better path anyway; I reached for `osascript` out of habit. You can just dismiss the dialog with Don't Allow.

One other thing the screenshot revealed: the bridge's `navigate` reported `title: "Lobu"` and returned a tab id, but the **visible** window is still on Hacker News. Bridge-driven tabs aren't necessarily the focused ones — so for recording I need `focus_tab`, not just `navigate`. Worth knowing before I trusted a capture that was filming the wrong tab.

**On the cursor** — it's not an overlay, it's baked in:

- `screencapture -C` captures the **real macOS cursor** into the video as pixels.
- `screencapture -k` draws **click indicators** in the recording — macOS's own version of testreel's click ripple.

The catch is what makes it move. `click_ref` through the Chrome bridge dispatches DOM events without touching the system pointer, so `-C` would film a cursor sitting motionless wherever it was left. Real motion needs `computer_use`'s `move_mouse`, which drives the actual pointer — then `-C` captures the travel and `-k` catches the click.

So three options, and I'd mix them:

| Beat | Method | Cursor |
|---|---|---|
| Map (3), Activity (4) | bridge `click_ref` | none — matches the spec, cursor is hidden during camera moves |
| Copy prompt (2a), Approve (5) | `computer_use` `move_mouse` + `click` | real pointer, real ripple |
| fallback | synthetic Remotion cursor over footage | full easing control, but must be hand-synced to the real click — fragile |

**Confidence: high (~90)** on the diagnosis — the dialog is visible in the screenshot and the exit-15 timeout matches it exactly. **Untested still:** frame rate under motion, and whether fullscreen gives a clean 1:1 frame. Both were in the command that stalled.

What I need from you: dismiss that dialog (Don't Allow is fine), and tell me whether the mini's Chrome is signed into the org you want filmed. Then I'll rerun the test with `computer_use` instead of AppleScript and we'll have the fps answer in one shot.

**Screenforge** is the only free alternative that directly matches Screen Studio's core capability: automatic zoom animations analyzed from cursor movement and click patterns, with no manual keyframing required. It's available on macOS now, with Windows coming.

## Paid Alternatives with Auto-Zoom and Smooth Cursor

**ScreenKite** allows users to record their screen and quickly generate demo-style videos with automatic cursor tracking and smooth zoom effects.

**Rapidemo** is the best fit if you want Screen Studio on Windows, with a lifetime license of $79 once for both Windows and macOS, with all updates included.

content.text:
Short answer: for our pipeline, the best cursor overlay isn't one we record — it's one we **generate**, because we're the thing moving the pointer.

Every `move_mouse` and `click` we issue through `computer_use` is a known `(t, x, y)` event. So the cursor track is an *output of the automation script*, not something to recover from the video. Record with the cursor **off**, log the positions we commanded, and draw the cursor in Remotion from that log. Three things fall out for free:

- **Perfect sync by construction** — no hand-matching a drawn cursor to a real click.
- **Easing.** The real pointer *teleports* between `move_mouse` targets, which looks awful on camera. A synthetic one can ease along a curve — the exact reason testreel draws its own.
- **The same data drives the camera.** Auto-zoom-to-cursor is what Screen Studio infers from movement; we don't have to infer it, we already know where the click is going.

That said, the capture layer is worth upgrading from raw `screencapture`:

**[aperture-node](https://github.com/wulkano/aperture-node)** (the recorder behind Kap) is the one I'd reach for — a Node API over ScreenCaptureKit with `showCursor`, `highlightClicks`, crop region, fps and codec. The real win over `screencapture` isn't the cursor flags we already have, it's **programmatic start/stop**: a recording can span exactly one beat, driven by the script, instead of guessing a `-V` duration up front. [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/aperture/v/3.0.0) · [Swift core](https://github.com/wulkano/Aperture)

**[node-mac-recorder](https://github.com/aslanon/node-mac-recorder)** is the alternative worth knowing, mainly for window selection and automatic overlay-window exclusion — useful if we decide against fullscreen and want to capture just the Chrome window.

The Screen Studio-likes — **[OpenScreen](https://www.opentechhub.io/openscreen/)** (MIT, auto-zoom + smooth cursor), **[Screenforge](https://screenforgeai.com/blogs/screen-studio-alternatives/)** — do the polished-cursor thing well, but they're GUI apps that own the whole edit. They'd *replace* the Remotion composition, not feed it, and we'd lose the authored camera and the 19-caption script. Wrong shape for this film, right shape if you ever want a quick one-off product clip.

So: `aperture-node` for capture control, our own cursor track rendered in Remotion, and skip the recorder apps.

**Confidence: medium (~65).** The capability claims come from the projects' own docs, and I have *not* verified `aperture` builds on macOS 26.6 or installs cleanly on the mini — that's a real risk with a native ScreenCaptureKit addon on a very new OS. Worth a 10-minute install test before committing.

content.text:
Because they're for a **machine to look at, not a human**. The manifest makes it explicit:

```
observe   Capture the target and inspect its accessibility tree. Returns screenshot
          metadata, optional PNG base64, UI elements, and a snapshot_id for later
          element-targeted actions.
click     Click an element id, query, or coordinates.
```

That's a perception→action loop. `observe` hands a model the current state, the model picks an element, `click` takes the `element id` from that same snapshot. One frame, consumed in one turn, then discarded. The giveaway is `optional PNG base64` — the image is the *optional* part. The accessibility tree is usually the real payload, because a tree of labelled elements is far better than pixels for deciding what to click.

Video is the opposite shape in every dimension. It's continuous rather than a point in time, it's for a human watching later rather than a model deciding now, and its value lives in the *motion between* states rather than in any single state. For an agent it would also be strictly worse: sixty frames a second of a mostly-static screen is sixty times the tokens carrying the same information.

So it isn't an oversight — the two capabilities have opposite consumers, and the platform built the one its agents needed. The gap only appears the moment you want a human-facing artifact out of a machine built for agent perception, which is exactly what we're doing tonight. That's also why adding it is a genuine product capability rather than demo scaffolding: "show me what the agent did" is a human question, and right now nothing can answer it.

ran bash, curl, and file writes. Headless `run` has no surface to prompt on, so an `ask` permission
can never be answered — the effective states collapse to "allow" or "tool removed". Removing
`--auto` buys nothing; keep it so the full-trust posture is explicit rather than accidental.

**Per-tool denies are theater while bash is open.** Denying `webfetch` blocks opencode's *built-in
webfetch tool*, not network access — `curl` through the allowed bash tool fetched the page anyway.

content.content:
guard let operation = job.operation_key else {
            throw ComputerUseError.invalidJob("Action job missing operation_key")
        }
        let input = job.action_input ?? [:]
        let output: [String: Any]
        switch operation {
        case "permissions": output = try await permissions()
        case "list_apps": output = try listAppsNative()
        case "list_windows": output = try await listWindows(input)
        case "screenshot": output = try screenshotNative(input)
        case "observe": output = try await observe(input)
        case "click": output = try await click(input)
        case "type_text": output = try typeTextNative(input)
        case "paste_text": output = try pasteTextNative(input)
        case "hotkey": output = try hotkeyNative(input)
        case "move_mouse": output = try moveMouseNative(input)
        case "scroll":
            output = (input.string("target") != nil || input.string("snapshot_id") != nil)
                ? try await scrollViaPeekaboo(input)
                : try scrollNative(input)
        case "focus_window":
            output = input.string("window_title") != nil
                ? try await focusWindowViaPeekaboo(input)
                : try focusWindowNative(input)
        case "launch_app": output = try launchAppNative(input)
        default:
            throw ComputerUseError.invalidJob("Unsupported apple.computer_use action '\(operation)'")
        }
        var withMeta = output
        withMeta["operation_key"] = operation
        withMeta["success"] = true
        let usesPeekaboo = operation == "observe"
            || (operation == "click" && input.double("x") == nil)
            || (operation == "scroll" && (input.string("target") != nil || input.string("snapshot_id") != nil))
            || (operation == "focus_window" && input.string("window_title") != nil)
        withMeta["backend"] = usesPeekaboo ? "peekaboo_cli" : "macos_native"
        return withMeta.mapValues { AnyEncodable($0) }
    }

    private func permissions() async throws -> [String: Any] {
        // Probe Owletto's own TCC identity — not the Peekaboo subprocess, which
        // carries a separate bundle id and reports false even when Owletto is granted.
        [
            "success": true,
            "data": [
                "permissions": [
                    permissionRow(
                        "Screen Recording",
                        isGranted: CGPreflightScreenCaptureAccess(),
                        isRequired: true,
                        grantInstructions: "System Settings > Privacy & Security > Screen Recording"
                    ),
                    permissionRow(
                        "Accessibility",
                        isGranted: AXIsProcessTrusted(),
                        isRequired: true,
                        grantInstructions: "System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility"
                    ),
                    permissionRow(
                        "Event Synthesizing",
                        isGranted: CGPreflightPostEventAccess(),
                        isRequired: false,
                        grantInstructions: "System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility"
                    ),
                ],
                "source": "macos_preflight",
            ],
        ]
    }

    private func permissionRow(
        _ name: String,
        isGranted: Bool,
        isRequired: Bool,
        grantInstructions: String
    ) -> [String: Any] {

---
name: project_owletto_observe_wedges_device_worker
description: "apple.computer_use `observe` permanently wedges the Mac device worker — it shells out to the peekaboo CLI with no timeout, peekaboo blocks on its bridge host, and the worker never polls again while Owletto.app keeps running and looking healthy"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
---

Diagnosed 2026-08-06 on Burak's Mac mini while trying to capture demo-video footage. **Not fixed yet.**

## Symptom

The device stops claiming runs (`Run N was never claimed within 60000ms — device "Burak's Mac mini" last polled Xm ago`) while `Owletto.app` stays running with a normal uptime. Nothing looks wrong from the outside; the menu bar app is up.

## Evidence

`~/Library/Logs/Owletto/owletto.log` — the last line before the device goes dark was `executing observe` **both times**:

```
21:43:58 [INFO] [worker] executing run
21:44:18 [INFO] [worker] executing observe     ← then dark for 5 hours
...
04:11:37 [INFO] [worker] executing focus_window
04:11:47 [INFO] [worker] executing observe     ← then dark until restart
```

Only a restart of Owletto.app brings it back (`[app] launch …` then `capabilities=[computer_use, os.shell, reminders]`).

## Mechanism

`apps/mac/Owletto/MacComputerUseActionService.swift`:

- `case "observe": output = try await observe(input)` (~line 40)
- `let usesPeekaboo = operation == "observe" || …` (~line 61) — **observe ALWAYS goes through the peekaboo CLI subprocess**, reported as `backend: "peekaboo_cli"`. `click` without x/y, `scroll` with target/snapshot_id, and `focus_window` with `window_title` take the same path.
- The subprocess appears to have **no timeout**, so a blocked peekaboo holds the worker's execution slot forever.

Why peekaboo blocks: it resolves permissions through a **"Peekaboo Bridge" host app** with its own bundle id, not Owletto's. Run from a context without the grant it reports:

```
Screen Recording (Required): Not Granted
Accessibility (Required): Not Granted
Hint: Grant Screen Recording to that host app, or run capture commands with
      --no-remote --capture-engine cg when the caller process already has permission
```

The `permissions` op already knows about this split — its comment says it probes "Owletto's own TCC identity — not the Peekaboo subprocess, which carries a separate bundle id and reports false even when Owletto is granted."

## My earlier diagnosis was WRONG

I first blamed a `503 no available server` on `/api/workers/poll`. The log shows those 503s and `reconcileFolderFeeds` 404s running **continuously** without killing the loop. The death correlates with `observe`, twice out of twice. See [[feedback_verify_dont_reason_from_construction]].

## Fix directions (none implemented)

1. **Bound the subprocess.** A single operation must never be able to hold the worker loop indefinitely — timeout + kill + return a terminal failure. This is the real fix; everything else is mitigation.
2. **Preflight before invoking peekaboo**, so a missing grant fails fast instead of hanging.
3. Consider `--no-remote --capture-engine cg` so peekaboo uses Owletto's own (granted) TCC identity rather than its bridge host.

Relates to [[reference_device_online_window_and_liveness_diagnosis]] — the device looks online while being functionally dead.

## Workaround while unfixed

Avoid `observe` entirely, and avoid `focus_window` with `window_title`. Focus apps with `os.shell` → `open -a "<App>"` instead, and verify state with `screencapture -x` rather than `observe`. See [[reference_mac_mini_screen_capture_rig]].

---
name: reference_mac_mini_screen_capture_rig
description: "How to record real 1920x1080@60 screen video on Burak's Mac mini — Owletto os.shell holds the Screen Recording grant (SSH does not), tmux over SSH drives the terminal, Ghostty fullscreen gives a clean frame"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
---

Proven 2026-08-06. The mini (`ssh mini` → `buraks-mac-mini.brill-kanyu.ts.net`) is the capture machine. Its display is **exactly 1920×1080 @ 60Hz at 1:1**, which matches a 1080p60 composition natively — no scaling.

## The permission split (the whole reason this is non-obvious)

```
kTCCServiceScreenCapture | com.owletto.mac              | 2  ← GRANTED
kTCCServiceAccessibility | com.owletto.mac              | 2  ← GRANTED
kTCCServiceScreenCapture | com.apple.Terminal           | 2  ← GRANTED
kTCCServiceAccessibility | /usr/libexec/sshd-keygen-wrapper | 0  ← DENIED
```

(read with `sqlite3 "/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db" "select service, client, auth_value from access where …"`)

**`screencapture` over SSH fails** with `could not create image from display` — TCC attributes it to `sshd`. **It works through Owletto's `os.shell`**, because that runs inside a GUI app that holds the grant. Same for `peekaboo` (`Operation desktopObservation is not allowed`).

## The rig

| Job | Tool | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Drive the terminal | `ssh mini` + `tmux send-keys -t reel` | Lands every time; no focus fights, no TCC |
| Verify terminal state | `tmux capture-pane -t reel -p` | Text, cheap, exact — better than a screenshot |
| Record pixels | Owletto `os.shell` → `screencapture` | Only path with the grant |
| Clean frame | Ghostty fullscreen (`cmd+ctrl+f`) | No menu bar, Dock, or wallpaper |

Create the tmux session **through `os.shell`**, not SSH, so child processes inherit the GUI session's keychain (that is what lets `claude` authenticate). Then drive it with `send-keys` over SSH.

```
tmux new-session -d -s reel -x 210 -y 52 -c ~/demo; tmux set -t reel status off
open -na Ghostty --args -e /opt/homebrew/bin/tmux attach -t reel
```

## screencapture flags that matter

```
-C   capture the cursor       -k   show clicks (macOS's own click ripple)
-v   video                    -V<n> limit to n seconds (omit and SIGINT to stop)
-x   no sound  -D<n> pick display
```

Stop an open-ended recording with `pkill -INT -f "screencapture -v"`.

## Two real limits

- **VFR, ~5 fps on static content.** A 549 s capture produced 2726 frames (`avg_frame_rate` ≈ 4.96) even though the container says `60/1` — it only encodes on change. Fine for terminal text; choppy for real motion.
- **No zoom, and no headroom.** The panel is 1080p at 1:1, so any push in post softens. Zoom **at capture time** instead (browser zoom, bigger Ghostty font) and let the compositor only ever scale down.

## Traps

- Ghostty restores its previous window on relaunch, so a changed `command =` in `~/.config/ghostty/config` won't apply — launch with `open -na Ghostty --args -e <cmd>`.
- `window-decoration = false` breaks native fullscreen. Leave it out.
- `osascript`/System Events from Owletto's shell hits an **Automation consent prompt** that blocks for ~60 s and then times out. Use `computer_use` ops or `open -a` instead.
- Owletto prompts "would like to access data from other apps" on **every launch** — it sits centre-screen and lands in frame. Dismiss before capturing.
- Never use `observe` — it wedges the worker permanently. See [[project_owletto_observe_wedges_device_worker]].
- The Dock reveals when the pointer nears the bottom edge; park it mid-screen with `move_mouse`.

## Staging (reversible)

```
defaults write com.apple.finder CreateDesktop false; killall Finder       # hide desktop icons
defaults write com.apple.dock autohide -bool true; killall Dock
defaults write com.apple.WindowManager StandardHideWidgets -int 1; killall WindowManager
```
Revert by setting `true`/`false`/`0` respectively. Better than all of it: run the app **fullscreen**, which removes menu bar, Dock, widgets and wallpaper at once and gives a 1:1 frame.

---
name: project_lobu_demo_reel
description: "The 90s Lobu demo reel for CTO/VP Eng — Remotion project at ~/Code/lobu-reel, composition spec artifact, 1 of 10 cards shot for real so far, what's blocked"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
---

Started 2026-08-06. Goal: a **90-second** demo film for CTO / VP Eng buyers whose argument is *every agent, in every harness, writes to and reads from the same governed context, and humans stay in the loop where they already work*.

## Where things live

- **Remotion project: `~/Code/lobu-reel`** (deliberately outside the monorepo). `bun install`, `bunx remotion studio`, `bunx remotion render Reel out/x.mp4`. Remotion 4.0.506 + `@remotion/media`.
- **Composition spec artifact**: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/38682b03-7752-4d1b-bc48-4e7ca182b1ae — beat sheet, frame wireframes, animation grammar, pipeline, continuity checklist.
- Renders in `out/`; captures in `public/capture/`.

## The composition

Six beats over 90 s: cold open (Slack answer) → setup (agent scaffolds Lobu) → the map (connectors/agents/behaviors/memory) → causality (Codex writes, Activity receives) → payoff (Slack Q&A, approval card rewrites itself) → close.

Key structural decision, in `src/lib/`: **cards never move, the camera does.** Every card has one permanent address in a 4200×1900 "table" (`layout.ts`); `camera.ts` holds ~14 keyframes that pan/push across it; `timing.ts` holds beat boundaries and the four allowed moves (camera 320ms, handoff 420ms, packet 200ms, caption 180/140ms). One easing curve throughout. The close pulls back to show every card at once, so the layout *is* the final frame. Captions carry the whole argument (no VO) — asserted at module load to be ≤7 words and ≥1.2 s.

`CaptureCard.tsx` swaps a grey-box `Card` for real footage; testreel's chrome is NOT used because Remotion draws the window.

## Status: 1 of 10 cards is real

**Shot**: beat 2's middle shot — Claude Code (Sonnet 5) on the mini scaffolding a real Lobu project with `npx @lobu/cli@latest init`. 9m10s raw at `public/capture/beat-setup.mov`. Nice arc: it refuses to install an unverified package, runs `npm view`, discovers Burak is the maintainer, then proceeds. Real files land (`lobu.config.ts`, `AGENTS.md`, `agents/demo/{IDENTITY,SOUL,USER}.md`).

**Everything else is grey boxes.** Renders `out/animatic.mp4` (all mock) and `out/animatic-v2.mp4` (one real card).

## Blocked on Burak

- Owletto's "access data from other apps" dialog sits centre-screen on the mini on every launch — lands in frame.
- **Slack is signed out on the mini** — blocks beats 1 and 5, which are the film's opening and payoff.
- **opencode has 0 credentials** on the mini (`opencode auth login`). Claude Code works and was used instead.

## Editorial debts

- 9m10s of footage for a 20 s beat: speed-ramping alone won't do it (4× still leaves 2m15s). Needs three selected moments — prompt, scaffold running, file tree — not one window.
- Terminal text is marginal at card scale. Fix at capture time (bigger Ghostty font), not by pushing the camera — see the no-headroom limit in [[reference_mac_mini_screen_capture_rig]].

## Tooling verdicts

- **testreel** (Playwright recorder) — installed then dropped. Needs a 127 MB headless Chromium and a storageState export; the Owletto bridge drives the *real logged-in* Chrome instead.
- **brainless** (shadcn agent-UI registry) — was going to fake the terminal panes; unnecessary once real terminals became recordable.
- **Screen Studio** — installed on the mini. Great smooth-cursor/auto-zoom, but a GUI app that would *replace* the composition rather than feed it. Possible hybrid: use it as the capture+cursor layer, export flat, composite in Remotion.
- Cursor: `screencapture -C/-k` bakes in the real cursor and click ripples, but `click_ref` through the Chrome bridge doesn't move the pointer. Since we *drive* the pointer, the cursor track is an output of the script — render it in Remotion from known positions rather than recovering it from video.

Capture recipe: [[reference_mac_mini_screen_capture_rig]]. Blocking bug: [[project_owletto_observe_wedges_device_worker]].

- 9m10s of footage for a 20 s beat: speed-ramping alone won't do it (4× still leaves 2m15s). Needs three selected moments — prompt, scaffold running, file tree — not one window.
- Terminal text is marginal at card scale. Fix at capture time (bigger Ghostty font), not by pushing the camera — see the no-headroom limit in [[reference_mac_mini_screen_capture_rig]].

## Tooling verdicts

- **testreel** (Playwright recorder) — installed then dropped. Needs a 127 MB headless Chromium and a storageState export; the Owletto bridge drives the *real logged-in* Chrome instead.
- **brainless** (shadcn agent-UI registry) — was going to fake the terminal panes; unnecessary once real terminals became recordable.
- **Screen Studio** — installed on the mini. Great smooth-cursor/auto-zoom, but a GUI app that would *replace* the composition rather than feed it. Possible hybrid: use it as the capture+cursor layer, export flat, composite in Remotion.
- Cursor: `screencapture -C/-k` bakes in the real cursor and click ripples, but `click_ref` through the Chrome bridge doesn't move the pointer. Since we *drive* the pointer, the cursor track is an output of the script — render it in Remotion from known positions rather than recovering it from video.

Capture recipe: [[reference_mac_mini_screen_capture_rig]]. Blocking bug: [[project_owletto_observe_wedges_device_worker]].

content.text:
Confirmed — and you're right to be surprised. Four ops shell out to the **peekaboo CLI**; everything else is native:

```swift
"observe"      → peekaboo see --path … --capture-engine classic
"click"        → peekaboo click        (only when x/y are absent)
"scroll"       → peekaboo scroll       (only with target/snapshot_id)
"focus_window" → peekaboo window focus (only with window_title)
```

And here is the actual bug, in `runPeekabooJSON`:

```swift
try proc.run()
proc.waitUntilExit()      // ← no timeout, ever
```

An unbounded `waitUntilExit()`. peekaboo triggers a TCC consent prompt for the target app — that's the "Owletto would like to access data from other apps" dialog we keep seeing — the prompt waits for a human, the process never exits, and the worker's execution slot is held forever. Exactly what the `os.shell` timeout hint warned about: *"blocks on a consent prompt that waits for someone at the machine, which on an unattended Mac can be hours."*

Worth noting the code already passes `--no-remote` specifically to dodge the peekaboo daemon ("so users grant TCC once on Owletto") — so the intent was already to avoid this. It just doesn't survive the prompt.

Checking how much of `observe` Owletto could do natively:

That splits into two different pieces of work, and only one is the bug:

**The bug is the missing timeout.** A hung subprocess must never be able to hold the worker's slot forever — that's true regardless of *which* subprocess. ~15 lines in `runPeekabooJSON`, and it fixes `observe`, `click`, `scroll` and `focus_window` at once.

**Removing peekaboo is a separate improvement.** A native `observe` needs an `AXUIElement` tree walk plus a snapshot store so `click --on element_id` can resolve ids — roughly 150–250 lines, and it's a feature, not a fix.

content.rawContent:
<!-- Per-repo agent rules loaded into every Claude Code session in this repo. Inlines AGENTS.md (shared project rules) first, then layers local-only notes below. User memory entries live under ~/.claude/projects/.../memory/. Don't add anything here unless it's only relevant to Claude agent specific. If other harnesses like pi or codex need it, modify AGENTS.md -->

@AGENTS.md

content.content:
## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source is in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- Main packages: `core` shared types/utils, `plugin-api` native plugin contracts, `plugin-host` deterministic plugin composition, `server` gateway + embedded runtime, `agent-worker` Lobu agent execution, `connectors` built-in connectors, `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Before editing a package, read its nearest `AGENTS.md` if present.
- `docs/GOTCHAS.md` collects the mechanical traps (build, SQL, testing, submodule, browser) that have each cost a debugging session. Skim the section for the surface you are touching before you start, and grep it when something looks inexplicable.

## Hard invariants
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly — work in a worktree.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout.
- One branch = one concern (not one file). Tangential task → commit/push/open current work, then branch fresh from `main`. Split only for genuinely independent concerns or an unreviewable diff.
- **Multi-replica correctness is mandatory.** Never put shared required state in an in-memory Map/singleton another replica must read or mutate. If a feature relies on cross-pod visibility, use Postgres-mediated state/signal.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone/supersede instead.
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** Connector resyncs can supersede a row and allocate a new id for the same source item. Cross-sync identity and dedupe must use the connector's stable `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key, never `events.id`.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over an append-only / run-history table (`events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, …) on a user-facing read path. History only grows, so read-time aggregation cost grows with it while the answer stays bounded. Materialize the row or counter at WRITE time and read it back by index; run the one-time aggregation in a migration, never per request. Aggregating bounded config tables (`connections`, `watchers`, `agent_users`) is fine.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are frequently real human signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Workers never receive real credentials.** They may receive only placeholders/proxied access. The only exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived credential leases (see `packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one of them.
- Default to static `import`. New dynamic imports require measured cost justification here or in the package AGENTS plus a rationale comment at the call site. Tests may dynamically import after mocks.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Compile and run every standalone Swift test under apps/mac/Tests/.
#
# The Mac app has no XCTest target — Owletto.xcodeproj carries a single
# `Owletto` scheme — so each test here is a self-contained `@main` executable
# that compiles the production sources it exercises and nothing else. That is
# what keeps them fast (no SwiftUI app graph, no simulator), but it also means
# nothing discovers them: until this script they only ran when a human pasted
# the swiftc line out of a file header.
#
# The build command is read from that same header comment rather than from a
# separate manifest, so the documented invocation IS the executed one and the
# two cannot drift apart.
#
# A test file whose header carries no swiftc block is an error, not a skip.
# Otherwise the failure mode is silent: a new test joins the directory, never
# runs, and reads as covered.
#
# Usage:
#   apps/mac/Tests/run-tests.sh              # every test
#   apps/mac/Tests/run-tests.sh TurnPrompt   # only files matching a substring

set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../.."

filter="${1:-}"
build_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$build_dir"' EXIT

# Pull the swiftc invocation out of the header comment: start at the `swiftc`
# line, keep going while lines continue with a trailing backslash, stop at the
# `&& /tmp/...` run tail.
extract_build_command() {
    awk '
        /^\/\/[[:space:]]*swiftc/ { collecting = 1 }
        collecting {
            line = $0
            sub(/^\/\/[[:space:]]*/, "", line)
            sub(/\\[[:space:]]*$/, "", line)
            printf "%s ", line
            if (line ~ /&&/) exit
            if ($0 !~ /\\[[:space:]]*$/) exit
        }
    ' "$1"
}

passed=0
failed=0
failing_tests=""

for test_file in apps/mac/Tests/*.swift; do
    name="$(basename "$test_file" .swift)"
    if [ -n "$filter" ] && ! echo "$name" | grep -q "$filter"; then
        continue
    fi

    raw="$(extract_build_command "$test_file")"
    if [ -z "$raw" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file has no 'swiftc' block in its header comment."
        echo "       Add the invocation that builds it so this runner can find it."
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    # Drop the `&& /tmp/binary` tail — this script runs the binary itself.
    command_head="${raw%%&&*}"

    read -ra tokens <<<"$command_head"
    if [ "${tokens[0]}" != "swiftc" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file header builds with '${tokens[0]}', not swiftc."
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    # Rebuild the argument list rather than eval'ing the comment: keep flags,
    # require every non-flag token to be a real file, and supply our own -o.
    args=()
    sources=""
    skip_next=0
    bad_token=""
    for token in "${tokens[@]:1}"; do
        if [ "$skip_next" -eq 1 ]; then
            skip_next=0
            continue
        fi
        if [ "$token" = "-o" ]; then
            skip_next=1
            continue
        fi
        case "$token" in
            -*)
                args+=("$token")
                ;;
            *)
                if [ ! -f "$token" ]; then
                    bad_token="$token"
                    break
                fi
                args+=("$token")
                sources="$sources $token"
                ;;
        esac
    done

    if [ -n "$bad_token" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file header names a source that does not exist: $bad_token"
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    # The header must actually compile the test it heads. A copy-pasted block
    # pointing at a different file would otherwise run its neighbour twice and
    # report this one green.
    case " $sources " in

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Compile and run every standalone Swift test under apps/mac/Tests/.
#
# The Mac app has no XCTest target — Owletto.xcodeproj carries a single
# `Owletto` scheme — so each test here is a self-contained `@main` executable
# that compiles the production sources it exercises and nothing else. That is
# what keeps them fast (no SwiftUI app graph, no simulator), but it also means
# nothing discovers them: until this script they only ran when a human pasted
# the swiftc line out of a file header.
#
# The build command is read from that same header comment rather than from a
# separate manifest, so the documented invocation IS the executed one and the
# two cannot drift apart.
#
# A test file whose header carries no swiftc block is an error, not a skip.
# Otherwise the failure mode is silent: a new test joins the directory, never
# runs, and reads as covered.
#
# Usage:
#   apps/mac/Tests/run-tests.sh              # every test
#   apps/mac/Tests/run-tests.sh TurnPrompt   # only files matching a substring

set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../.."

filter="${1:-}"
build_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$build_dir"' EXIT

# Pull the swiftc invocation out of the header comment: start at the `swiftc`
# line, keep going while lines continue with a trailing backslash, stop at the
# `&& /tmp/...` run tail.
extract_build_command() {
    awk '
        /^\/\/[[:space:]]*swiftc/ { collecting = 1 }
        collecting {
            line = $0
            sub(/^\/\/[[:space:]]*/, "", line)
            sub(/\\[[:space:]]*$/, "", line)
            printf "%s ", line
            if (line ~ /&&/) exit
            if ($0 !~ /\\[[:space:]]*$/) exit
        }
    ' "$1"
}

passed=0
failed=0
failing_tests=""

for test_file in apps/mac/Tests/*.swift; do
    name="$(basename "$test_file" .swift)"
    if [ -n "$filter" ] && ! echo "$name" | grep -q "$filter"; then
        continue
    fi

    raw="$(extract_build_command "$test_file")"
    if [ -z "$raw" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file has no 'swiftc' block in its header comment."
        echo "       Add the invocation that builds it so this runner can find it."
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    # Drop the `&& /tmp/binary` tail — this script runs the binary itself.
    command_head="${raw%%&&*}"

    read -ra tokens <<<"$command_head"
    if [ "${tokens[0]}" != "swiftc" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file header builds with '${tokens[0]}', not swiftc."
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    # require every non-flag token to be a real file, and supply our own -o.
    args=()
    sources=""
    skip_next=0
    bad_token=""

content.text: Good instinct — let me look at how Claude's own computer-use tool is shaped rather than invent the contract.

That's a useful reference point. Claude's computer-use has **no accessibility tree at all** — no `observe`, no `element_id`. It's `screenshot` → model reads coordinates off that image → `left_click(coordinate)`, with `zoom` as a read-only tool for small text. Codex's CUA works the same way.

Two things I'm taking from it:

- **Coordinates must always work as the fallback**, since that's the only universal path — our `clickNative(x, y)` already is that, so the AX tree stays an optimization rather than a dependency.
- **`computer_batch` is the thing we're missing.** Claude batches a predictable sequence into one call explicitly because "each individual tool call requires a model→API round trip (seconds)". That's exactly why driving the mini has been so slow tonight — focus → hotkey → move_mouse → screenshot is four device round-trips, ~30 s. Different concern from this branch, but worth its own.

content.text:
Checked with evidence — and the answer is there's nothing to copy:

```
codex-cli 0.146.1 → native binaries
  AXUIElement / CGWindowList / ScreenCaptureKit symbol hits: 0, 0, 0
```

Codex ships **zero** accessibility or screen-capture code; it's a terminal coding agent. And Claude's computer-use, as we saw, deliberately has no AX tree either — screenshot plus coordinates, because that generalises across every app while AX metadata quality varies wildly (Electron apps in particular expose very little).

So nobody mainstream is shipping an AX-tree implementation to crib. Our `observe` design came from peekaboo. What I've built keeps **coordinates as the universal path** (matching Claude/Codex) and treats the AX tree as an optimisation on top — a superset rather than a bet on AX.

Since the whole point of this fix is the *bounds*, let me make them directly testable rather than buried behind live AX calls:

content.text:
ChatGPT.app takes a **third approach** — `NSAppleEventsUsageDescription`: *"ChatGPT uses Apple Events to control Mac apps on your behalf."* No AX symbols in its binary. So the field is:

| | Approach | Consent |
|---|---|---|
| Claude computer-use | screenshot + coordinates | screen recording, once |
| ChatGPT.app | Apple Events per app | **prompts per target app** |
| peekaboo (what we had) | AX tree via subprocess | prompts, own bundle id |
| this fix | AX tree in-process | accessibility, once |

Worth noting Apple Events is exactly what produced the blocking dialog when I tried `osascript` earlier — it prompts *per target app*, which is fine when a human is sitting there and fatal when unattended. AX is granted once, globally, which is why it's the right choice for a device worker.

**Five consecutive `observe` calls across five different apps — all succeeded, no consent prompt, and the worker is still polling afterwards:**

```

Before this change, *one* `observe` took the device down permanently. And note the reinstall kept `Screen Recording=true, Accessibility=true` — signing with the matching Developer ID identity avoided the TCC-record trap.

**What changed** (worktree `.claude/worktrees/mac-peekaboo-timeout/`, owletto submodule):

- `MacAccessibilityTree.swift` — new. In-process AX tree with two hard bounds: `AXUIElementSetMessagingTimeout` per call, plus a whole-walk deadline and element cap. Plus a bounded snapshot store and element resolution.
- `MacComputerUseNative.swift` — `observeNative`, `clickElementNative`, `scrollTargetNative`, `focusWindowByTitleNative`, and one shared `enumerateWindows`.
- `MacComputerUseActionService.swift` — **deleted `runPeekabooJSON`, `resolvePeekabooBinary`, `bundledPeekabooBinaryPath`, `isRunnableExecutable`** and the four peekaboo call sites. `backend` is now always `macos_native`. Renamed `peekabooFailed` → `platformFailed`, dropped the now-unreachable `peekabooMissing`.
- `AccessibilityTreeTests.swift` — 23 assertions, mutation-tested.

**Evidence:** 23/23 assertions pass; removing the deadline check fails the suite (`got 10000` — the unbounded behaviour); never setting `truncated` fails 2; restored passes. Full Mac suite 16/16. `xcodebuild` succeeds.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - Remotion 4.0.506 (`<Composition>`, `<Sequence>`, `useCurrentFrame`, `@remotion/media` `<Video>`, `interpolate`, `Easing.bezier`)
   - Composition architecture: **cards never move, the camera does** — fixed table space, camera keyframes, contain-fit
   - macOS TCC: per-app grants; `sqlite3 /Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db`; TCC pins a **code requirement** per approval, so a signing-identity change permanently invalidates grants
   - `screencapture` flags: `-v` video, `-V<n>` duration, `-C` cursor, `-k` click ripples, `-x` silent, `-D<n>` display
   - Owletto device bridge: `client.operations.execute({connection_id, operation_key, input})` — `os.shell` (464), `apple.computer_use` (447), `chrome` (479/432)
   - tmux as a control channel: `tmux send-keys` over SSH drives, `tmux capture-pane -p` verifies as text
   - Swift: `AXUIElement`, `AXUIElementSetMessagingTimeout`, `AXUIElementCopyAttributeValue`, `CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo`, `CGPreflightScreenCaptureAccess`, `AXIsProcessTrusted`
   - Mac test convention: standalone `@main` executables with a `swiftc` block in the header comment, run by `apps/mac/Tests/run-tests.sh`
   - Computer-use design comparison: Claude = screenshot+coordinates (no AX); Codex CLI = no AX/screen code at all; ChatGPT.app = Apple Events (prompts per target app); peekaboo = AX tree via subprocess

3. **Files and Code Sections:**

   **`~/Code/lobu-reel/` (Remotion project, outside the monorepo)**
   - `src/lib/timing.ts` — `FPS=60`, `s(seconds)`, `MOVE` (camera 0.32s, handoff 0.42s, packet 0.2s, captionIn 0.18s, captionOut 0.14s), `EASE = Easing.bezier(0.22,1,0.36,1)`, `BEAT` boundaries, `TOTAL = s(90)`

     ```ts
     export const CAPTION_BAND = 190;
     export const cameraTransform = (rect, viewW, viewH) => {
       const stage = viewH - CAPTION_BAND;
       const scale = Math.min(viewW / rect.w, stage / rect.h);
       const cx = rect.x + rect.w / 2, cy = rect.y + rect.h / 2;
       return `translate(${viewW/2}px, ${stage/2}px) scale(${scale}) translate(${-cx}px, ${-cy}px)`;

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Compile and run every standalone Swift test under apps/mac/Tests/.
#
# The Mac app has no XCTest target — Owletto.xcodeproj carries a single
# `Owletto` scheme — so each test here is a self-contained `@main` executable
# that compiles the production sources it exercises and nothing else. That is
# what keeps them fast (no SwiftUI app graph, no simulator), but it also means
# nothing discovers them: until this script they only ran when a human pasted
# the swiftc line out of a file header.
#
# The build command is read from that same header comment rather than from a
# separate manifest, so the documented invocation IS the executed one and the
# two cannot drift apart.
#
# A test file whose header carries no swiftc block is an error, not a skip.
# Otherwise the failure mode is silent: a new test joins the directory, never
# runs, and reads as covered.
#
# Usage:
#   apps/mac/Tests/run-tests.sh              # every test
#   apps/mac/Tests/run-tests.sh TurnPrompt   # only files matching a substring

set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../.."

filter="${1:-}"
build_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$build_dir"' EXIT

# Pull the swiftc invocation out of the header comment: start at the `swiftc`
# line, keep going while lines continue with a trailing backslash, stop at the
# `&& /tmp/...` run tail.
extract_build_command() {
    awk '
        /^\/\/[[:space:]]*swiftc/ { collecting = 1 }
        collecting {
            line = $0
            sub(/^\/\/[[:space:]]*/, "", line)
            sub(/\\[[:space:]]*$/, "", line)
            printf "%s ", line
            if (line ~ /&&/) exit
            if ($0 !~ /\\[[:space:]]*$/) exit
        }
    ' "$1"
}

passed=0
failed=0
failing_tests=""

for test_file in apps/mac/Tests/*.swift; do
    name="$(basename "$test_file" .swift)"
    if [ -n "$filter" ] && ! echo "$name" | grep -q "$filter"; then
        continue
    fi

    raw="$(extract_build_command "$test_file")"
    if [ -z "$raw" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file has no 'swiftc' block in its header comment."
        echo "       Add the invocation that builds it so this runner can find it."
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    # Drop the `&& /tmp/binary` tail — this script runs the binary itself.
    command_head="${raw%%&&*}"

    read -ra tokens <<<"$command_head"
    if [ "${tokens[0]}" != "swiftc" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file header builds with '${tokens[0]}', not swiftc."
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    # Rebuild the argument list rather than eval'ing the comment: keep flags,
    # require every non-flag token to be a real file, and supply our own -o.
    args=()
    sources=""
    skip_next=0
    bad_token=""
    for token in "${tokens[@]:1}"; do
        if [ "$skip_next" -eq 1 ]; then
            skip_next=0
            continue
        fi
        if [ "$token" = "-o" ]; then
            skip_next=1
            continue
        fi
        case "$token" in
            -*)
                args+=("$token")
                ;;
            *)
                if [ ! -f "$token" ]; then
                    bad_token="$token"
                    break
                fi
                args+=("$token")
                sources="$sources $token"
                ;;
        esac
    done

    if [ -n "$bad_token" ]; then
        echo "ERROR: $test_file header names a source that does not exist: $bad_token"
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    # The header must actually compile the test it heads. A copy-pasted block
    # pointing at a different file would otherwise run its neighbour twice and
    # report this one green.
    case " $sources " in
        *" $test_file "*) ;;
        *)
            echo "ERROR: $test_file header does not compile $test_file."
            failed=$((failed + 1))
            failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
            continue
            ;;
    esac

    binary="$build_dir/$name"
    if ! swiftc "${args[@]}" -o "$binary" 2>&1; then
        echo "FAIL (build): $name"
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
        continue
    fi

    if "$binary"; then
        passed=$((passed + 1))
    else
        echo "FAIL (run): $name"
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        failing_tests="$failing_tests $name"
    fi
done

if [ "$passed" -eq 0 ] && [ "$failed" -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "ERROR: no tests matched${filter:+ filter '$filter'}."
    exit 1
fi

echo
echo "Swift standalone tests: $passed passed, $failed failed"
if [ "$failed" -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "Failing:$failing_tests"
    exit 1
fi

---
name: feedback_never_hot_swap_owletto_app_remotely
description: Replacing /Applications/Owletto.app over SSH used to brick the device worker via a main-thread TCC-blocked open; ROOT CAUSE FIXED 2026-07-30, remote swap now verified safe
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 259b2997-9a73-4761-987d-67f0a02cf9fe
  modified: 2026-07-30T22:54:03.915Z
---

**Status: root cause FIXED 2026-07-30 (branch `feat/menubar-perms`). Remote swap of
`/Applications/Owletto.app` was performed 4x that night on the Mac mini over SSH with zero
downtime.** Keep this file for the mechanism, not the prohibition.

**The original failure (2026-07-30, ~19:55 UTC).** Replacing the bundle took the mini's worker
offline and could NOT be restored remotely — restoring the byte-identical backup hung the OLD build
in the same frame, because TCC keys its record to bundle path + code identity and a different binary
there invalidates the entry for both. `pkill UserNotificationCenter`, killing the per-user `tccd`,
and `tccutil reset SystemPolicyAppData com.owletto.mac` all failed. Recovery needed a human at the
screen.

**Why it bricked — the real bug.** `AppState` is `@MainActor`. `currentCapabilities` is a *computed
property* that called `WhatsAppLocalSyncService.isAvailable()`, a blocking
`FileHandle(forReadingAtPath:)` on the WhatsApp group container. A new binary makes TCC re-evaluate,
so that `open()` blocks until a human answers a dialog — parking the menu bar, poll loop, heartbeat
and every other connector. `sample <pid>` showing 100% of samples in `__open` under that stack is the
fingerprint. **The language was never the problem; the placement was.** Same call from a background
thread is harmless.

**Fixes applied (all in `AppState.swift`):**
1. `whatsAppArchiveReadable` — cached flag, probed via `Task.detached`, read by
   `currentCapabilities`. Main actor never does I/O.
2. **Probe once per launch**, forced only on explicit grant / toggle. Critical: poll interval is
   `actionPollInterval = 10`s whenever computer use is active, so probing in `syncNow()` meant a TCC
   dialog **every 10 seconds** — the user answered and it reappeared. This was a real reported
   symptom, not theoretical.
3. `refreshFDAStatus()` had the identical bug (blocking `open` of `knowledgeC.db` on the main actor,
   every poll). Now detached + 60s throttle — it re-polls because FDA genuinely changes at runtime.
4. Operand order: `isAvailable() && !whatsAppDisabled` ran the probe BEFORE the kill switch, so the
   user-facing toggle could not prevent the hang. Flag now short-circuits first. Same fix applied to
   the `system_audio` check.

**Not a bug, checked:** `hasHealthKit` = `HealthKitSyncService.hasBeenRequested`, a UserDefaults
flag rather than a live query. Apple deliberately does not expose HealthKit *read* authorization
(it would leak health data by inference), so a stored flag is the standard workaround.

**Safe remote-swap recipe (verified 4x):** `ditto -c -k --sequesterRsrc --keepParent` → `scp` →
`ditto -x -k` on the target → `codesign -v --deep --strict` → back up the old bundle → quit → `ditto`
into `/Applications` → `open -a`. Then verify: `sample <pid>` main thread parked in
`_BlockUntilNextEventMatchingListInMode` (idle, healthy) and the `device_workers` row heartbeating.
Expect capabilities gated on TCC to drop until the user answers the prompt — the app stays alive and
they return on the next forced probe. That degradation is the fix working.

**Diagnosing without installing:** grep the binary — `strings Owletto | grep -F "<known literal>"`.
Absence is weak evidence (not all Swift literals land in `strings`); `cmp` against your own build is
decisive.

**Seeing the screen:** the computer-use MCP CANNOT drive Owletto (`LSUIElement` app →
`request_access` returns `not_installed`; see [[feedback_computer_use_cant_grant_owletto]]). But
plain `screencapture -x` via Bash works fine on the local Mac. Over SSH to the mini it fails with
"could not create image from display" — no window-server session.

**Opening the menu bar popover yourself (no human needed).** computer-use can't reach an
`LSUIElement` app, but AppleScript UI scripting can, because System Events carries its OWN
Accessibility grant — Owletto's missing grants are irrelevant:

```bash
osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to tell process "Owletto" \
  to click menu bar item 1 of menu bar 2'
screencapture -x /tmp/popover.png    # then crop/zoom to read the chips
osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to key code 53'   # Escape to close
```

`menu bar 2` is the status bar (`menu bar 1` is the system one). This closes the self-verification
loop: you can confirm a menu-bar UI change landed without asking the user to look. Verified
2026-07-30 — read the permission chips and confirmed a removed section was gone.

See [[project_device_behavior_exit_report_delivery]].
Shell cwd was reset to /Users/burakemre/Code/lobu
